knownFor: Presbyter, an elder and priest of the church, at Caesarea in Palestine, who built a library for his church and, Jerome says, copied most of Origen's works with his own hand. In the persecution he was tortured, held two whole years in prison and put to death about 310. Eusebius says the two friends wrote a Defense of Origen together.
shortDescription: Pamphilus was a presbyter, an elder and priest of the church, at Caesarea on the coast of Roman Palestine, who built a library for his church and, Jerome says, copied most of Origen's works by hand. He was put to death for his faith about 310, after two years in prison, and his friend Eusebius says the two of them wrote a Defense of Origen together.
datesNote: No old source gives the year of his birth. Eusebius dates the start of the persecution in Palestine to April in the nineteenth year of the emperor Diocletian, which is 303. He puts Pamphilus in prison in its fifth year, after the Nones of November, so late in 307 or soon after. Pamphilus died after two whole years in prison, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, a day in February, so about 310. Jerome says he died in the persecution of Maximinus. Jerome's Lives of Illustrious Men, which tells of his copying, is dated to the fourteenth year of the emperor Theodosius, so 392 or 393
placeNote: Caesarea, a port on the coast of Roman Palestine, where he was presbyter, set up a school, gathered his library, was held in prison and was put to death. The longer form of Eusebius's account of the martyrs, held only in a damaged Greek scan, says he came from Berytus, today's Beirut. Photius, writing more than five centuries later, says he studied at Alexandria under Pierius
role: Presbyter of Caesarea; library builder and copyist of Origen's books; martyr

keyWorks.title: Defense of Origen (Apologia pro Origene)
keyWorks.about: a book answering the charges made against Origen, written in the persecution to confessors, Christians who had held to the faith under trial, condemned to the mines of Palestine. It sets out Origen's own words, under his name, with the defender's replies between, and says Origen searched the Scriptures as far as his strength allowed and did not settle them as fixed doctrine. Photius says it had six books. Only the first survives, in the Latin of Rufinus of Aquileia, which the Library holds in two printings. Eusebius says he and Pamphilus did the work jointly; later writers differ on whose it is.

keyWorks.title: The library at Caesarea
keyWorks.about: a collection of sacred books for the church: the works of Origen and of other church writers, Eusebius says. Eusebius gave its catalog in his Life of Pamphilus, now lost, so that readers could learn which of Origen's works survived. Jerome says Pamphilus searched the whole world for books, bought every book Origen wrote at great cost, and gave them to the church at Caesarea.

keyWorks.title: Copies of Origen in his own hand
keyWorks.about: Jerome says he copied the greater part of Origen's works with his own hand, and that these were still kept in the library at Caesarea. Jerome also writes that he found twenty-five volumes of Origen's commentaries on the twelve prophets in Pamphilus's hand, which he guarded with joy. Photius says only that Pamphilus is said to have copied most of Origen's commentaries on Scripture.

traces: Eusebius sent readers to the library's catalog to learn which of Origen's works survived.
Jerome used the library. He writes that the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew was kept there, and that he found the six volumes of Eusebius's Defense of Origen there.

Jerome writes that the library was afterwards partly destroyed, and that two bishops of Caesarea, Acacius and later Euzoius, tried to restore it in parchment volumes. The second recovered many works and left an inventory.
Jerome says the churches of Palestine read the copies of the Greek Old Testament that Origen prepared and that Eusebius and Pamphilus published.

Rufinus of Aquileia put the first book of the Defense into Latin under Pamphilus's name, and it is all that survives of the work. About ninety years after Pamphilus died, Jerome complained that readers gave no heed to the bishops who condemned Origen as a heretic, one whose teaching the church condemns, since they thought a martyr had praised him.
Eusebius took Pamphilus's name as a surname. Jerome says it came from his friendship for the martyr, and Photius that Eusebius was an ardent admirer of Pamphilus.

Isidore of Seville, about three centuries later, says Pamphilus was the first among Christians to try to equal Pisistratus, the founder of a famous pagan library, in zeal for a sacred library, and that he had nearly thirty thousand volumes.
remembered: Eusebius calls him his dearest friend, a man thrice dear to him, and the most illustrious of the martyrs of his time. In the longer form of his account, held only in a damaged Greek scan, he calls him my master.
Eusebius calls him a most eloquent man, of truly philosophical life, and says he set up a school at Caesarea.

Eusebius writes that he shared his possessions with the needy. The longer form says he sold what came to him from his forebears, gave it all to the naked, the maimed and the poor, and lived without possessions.
Eusebius's lost Life of Pamphilus, as Jerome quotes it, says he gave what he could to poor lovers of books, and gave the holy Scriptures freely to keep, to women as well as men.
Eusebius writes that the twelve who died with him were counted worthy of the grace and number of the apostles, and that on their day the chief gate of the kingdom of heaven was opened to them.
Socrates of Constantinople, a historian of the fifth century, calls Pamphilus and Eusebius trustworthy witnesses for Origen, in their joint life of him and defense of him.
A Syriac chronicle written centuries later says he taught Eusebius, and Theophanes, in the ninth century, lists him among the martyrs as a presbyter of Caesarea.
Photius names Pamphilus and Pierius as holy teachers, honored above others as famed for martyrdom, though he says he does not accept all their views.

uncertain: His life rests on one friend. Nearly all of it comes from Eusebius, who admired him, in the Church History and the Martyrs of Palestine. Eusebius's Life of Pamphilus in three books is lost. Its one surviving passage is held only in Jerome's Latin, where Jerome quotes it against Pamphilus's authorship of the Defense.

Who wrote the Defense of Origen. Eusebius writes that he and Pamphilus did the work jointly. Jerome, in 392 or 393, listed it under Pamphilus's name. Rufinus put its first book into Latin as Pamphilus's, though he called it the book Pamphilus is said to have written. In his Letter 84, Jerome doubted that it was Pamphilus's, since no other work of his could be shown, and suggested it was by Didymus or someone else. He added that if Pamphilus wrote it, he wrote it before he became a martyr, and was counted worthy of martyrdom to wash away his one fault. Rufinus answered that Jerome no longer spared even the martyrs.

Jerome's later charge. About ten years after his catalog, by his own count, Jerome said the Defense was a work of Eusebius in six books, and called Eusebius the chief of the Arians. He said he had found the six volumes in the library at Caesarea, and that Rufinus had changed a few statements about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. He admitted he had once listed it under Pamphilus's name.

The other old witnesses on the Defense. Socrates calls it their joint defense, and also speaks of the books Pamphilus wrote in defense of Origen. Photius says it had six books, five written by Pamphilus in prison with Eusebius, and the sixth by Eusebius alone after Pamphilus's death. Jerome's own counts differ: in his Apology against Rufinus he says Rufinus translated the first of Eusebius's six books, and in Letter 84 that the book holds nearly the first thousand lines of Eusebius's sixth book.

Whether Eusebius was in prison with him. Photius says Pamphilus wrote the Defense in prison in the company of Eusebius. Eusebius never says he was imprisoned. He says only that the two did the work jointly.

Friend or teacher. Eusebius calls Pamphilus his dearest friend. Jerome calls Pamphilus the patron of Eusebius. That Pamphilus taught Eusebius is said only in a Syriac chronicle written centuries later.

The year of his death. No old source gives the year. Eusebius's own counts, the fifth year of the persecution and then two whole years in prison, end in February about 310. The exact year depends on how the years of the persecution are counted, and the old sources do not settle it.

Where he studied. Photius, more than five centuries later, says Pierius, head of the school of Christian teaching at Alexandria, was his teacher. The longer form of Eusebius's account says he was schooled at Berytus before he turned to the sacred writings, and names no teacher.

His birthplace and family. That he came from Berytus, of a noble family, and was distinguished in public office there, stands only in the longer form of Eusebius's account, held in damaged Greek with no other print. The Syriac of the longer form is not held. The shorter account, in English, does not give it.

The manner of his death. The shorter account says only that the governor punished Pamphilus and his companions like the others before them. The longer form in Greek says a capital sentence, and Photius says by the sword.

How much he copied. Jerome says the greater part of Origen's works, and Photius says he is said to have copied most of Origen's commentaries on Scripture. In Jerome's Latin, manu ejus says only in his hand, in a sentence about Pamphilus.

The end of Jerome's passage on the volumes. His Latin says Pamphilus seems to him to have marked them with the traces of his own blood. The English of the Library's Jerome volume has lines that seem traced in his blood. The Greek of Sophronius printed beside the Latin ends with the traces of his own suffering, read from a scan with letter faults.

Whose command the money-changers are. The Defense calls it only a command, to become approved money-changers who keep what is good. Origen, in his Commentary on John, calls it the command of Jesus, beside Paul's teaching to abstain from every form of evil. Dionysius of Alexandria, as Eusebius quotes him, calls it the apostolic voice.

Another book and another apology. Photius describes an anonymous defense of Origen in five volumes, which relies chiefly on Pamphilus and Eusebius. He judges that it mostly supports the charges against Origen, and lists fifteen charges it calls slanders, among them that souls pass from one body into another and that there is no eternal punishment. He describes the Defense of Pamphilus and Eusebius next, as a separate work.

Other writings. Gennadius lists among Rufinus's Latin translations a work of Pamphilus the Martyr Against the mathematicians, meaning astrologers. Nothing held says whether it is a lost work or another name for the Defense. An Exposition of the Chapters of the Acts of the Apostles is printed under his name in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, whose notice says others give it to Euthalius; it is not counted here.
Copies of the Bible. Notes in some Bible manuscripts, reported by editors, say Pamphilus and Eusebius corrected the copies. The manuscripts are not held, so the notes are not counted here.

The text of the Defense. The Greek is lost. Book I survives only in Rufinus's Latin, held in two rough scans that agree with each other, and no English of it is held. Jerome charged Rufinus with changing passages on the Son and the Holy Spirit. The passage quoted in the story is not on those subjects.

Jerome, letter to Marcella, in Rufinus's Apology: the library of sacred books for the church at Caesarea. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75: the greater part of Origen's works copied with his own hand.
Eusebius, Church History VII.1: Origen's death, in the century before. World census, Origen: the Bible scholar who taught at Alexandria and then at Caesarea.
Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 11.2: his devotion above all to the Divine Scriptures. Jerome, letter to Marcella: the search through the world for books, and all of Origen's bought at great cost.

Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine, introduction and 4.8: the letters to level the churches and burn the Scriptures, then the edicts that all should sacrifice. Martyrs of Palestine 7.1 and 7.4-6: the fifth year; the governor's test in rhetorical philosophy and learning; the order to sacrifice, the refusal, the threats ignored, the scrapings in his sides and prison with the confessors.
Eusebius, Church History VI.33.4: the Defense written by him and Pamphilus, with care, on account of faultfinders. Photius, Library, codex 118: five books written by Pamphilus in prison.

The Defense, Book I, in Rufinus's Latin: the charges that Origen said the soul existed before the body, and called Christ a mere man, or made his deeds happen only in seeming; Origen's words set out with replies between; the heading to the confessors condemned to the mines of Palestine; the pardon given to readers of pagan and heretics' books, the testers' skill, the command to become approved money-changers, and the shame of the heretics.

Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 11.1-2, 11.5 and 11.14: two whole years in prison, the new governor's question, the one answer and the sentence; twelve in all, Pamphilus the only presbyter. The longer form in Greek: a capital sentence. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 81: Eusebius's surname from Pamphilus.
Eusebius, Church History VI.32.3: the library's catalog, for Origen's works. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 3: the library at Caesarea, used in his day.

Rufinus, preface to his Latin of the Defense: its first book, under Pamphilus's name. Jerome, Apology against Rufinus I.10: readers give no heed to the bishops who condemn Origen, the heretic, since they think a martyr has praised him; written about ten years after his catalog, by his own count.

Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75, in Latin and in the English of 1892: the twenty-five volumes of Origen's commentaries on the twelve prophets in Pamphilus's hand, guarded like the wealth of Croesus, and the many thousand lines marked with the traces of his blood.
World census, Alexandrian Christianity: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: He handed out the holy Scriptures as well, and most readily, to keep and not only to read. He gave them to men, and to women too, when he saw they were devoted to reading. So he kept many books prepared, to give freely to anyone who wished whenever need called for it.
quotationOriginals.printed: He would not only lend them copies of the Holy Scriptures to read, but would give them most readily, and that not only to men, but to women also if he saw that they were given to reading. He therefore kept a store of manuscripts, so that he might be able to give them to those who wished for them whenever occasion demanded.
quotationOriginals.work: Eusebius, Life of Pamphilus III, as Jerome quotes it in the Apology against Rufinus I.9, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Eusebius's Greek is lost. The story's English is made from the Latin that Jerome quotes, held only in a scan with letter faults, so the printed English stands alone; it agrees with the Latin in sense. The Latin says to keep, where the English says lend and give.

quotationOriginals.modern: They think the command to become approved money-changers is wholly shut out for those who read Origen's books. Such money-changers know how to keep what is good and hold back from every kind of evil. If anyone is only seen reading his books, at once they drench him in the shame of the heretics.
quotationOriginals.printed: ab his vero, qui Origenis libros legunt, istud penitus exclusum putant esse mandatum, quo probabiles jubentur effici trapezitae, scientes quod bonum est retinere, ab omni autem se specie mala abstinere: sed tantum modo si legere libros illius visus fuerit, statim ab his haereticorum perfundetur infamia
quotationOriginals.work: The Defense of Origen, Book I, preface to the confessors, in Rufinus's Latin, ed. Lommatzsch
quotationOriginals.uncertain: No English of the Defense is held, so the story's English is made from this Latin. The Migne printing of the same Latin agrees, and reads si quis, if anyone, which the story's English follows. The Defense says this; whose words they are, Pamphilus's or Eusebius's, is disputed.

quotationOriginals.modern: If it is a joy to own one letter from a martyr, how much greater to own so many thousand lines! It seems to me he marked them with the traces of his own blood.
quotationOriginals.printed: And if it is such joy to have one epistle of a martyr how much more to have so many thousand lines which seem to me to be traced in his blood.
quotationOriginals.work: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The story's English is made from Jerome's Latin, which the Library holds only in a scan with letter faults, so the printed English stands alone. The Latin says Pamphilus seems to him to have marked them with the traces of his own blood. The Greek of Sophronius beside it, read from a scan with faults, ends with the traces of his own suffering.

lines.text: In April of the nineteenth year of the emperor Diocletian, letters go out in Palestine ordering the churches to be leveled and the Scriptures burned.
Later the governor Urbanus receives edicts that all the people in every city must sacrifice and pour offerings to the idols.

lines.text: After the Nones of November in the fifth year, Urbanus puts others in prison after severe tortures, and among them Pamphilus, whom Eusebius calls his dearest friend.

timeline.headline: The Defense of Origen
timeline.witness: The Defense itself, Book I, in Rufinus's Latin

lines.text: Eusebius writes that he and Pamphilus prepared the Defense with care and did the work jointly, on account of faultfinders.
lines.note: Photius says five of its six books were written by Pamphilus in prison, in the company of Eusebius (Photius, Library, codex 118, cic/texts/photius_library-v1_freese1920.txt lines 11437-11442).

lines.text: It is addressed to confessors condemned to the mines of Palestine.
It says some men condemn Origen from ignorance and others from malice, and turn on anyone who reads him, refusing his readers the pardon given to readers of pagan and even heretics' books.
It says that anyone only seen reading Origen's books is at once shamed as a heretic.
Its first argument is that Origen often says he is not giving a final verdict or fixed doctrine, but searching the Scriptures as far as his strength allows.
It sets out Origen's own words, under his name, with the defender's replies between.

lines.when: After two whole years in prison
lines.text: After two whole years in prison, five Egyptian Christians returning home are seized at the gates of Caesarea, and their arrival becomes the occasion of the martyrdom.
On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, the Egyptians are brought before the governor Firmilian, with Pamphilus and his companions.
The governor knows they have held firm under earlier tortures, and asks only whether they will now obey. Each gives the same answer, and he punishes them as he did the others.
lines.note: The longer form in Greek says a capital sentence (cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 25241-25244); Photius says by the sword (Library, codex 118, cic/texts/photius_library-v1_freese1920.txt lines 11440-11441).

lines.text: A young servant of his household, taught in his master's way of life, cries out from the crowd for the bodies to be buried. He is scraped and burned by slow fire, and dies before his master.
lines.note: Eusebius names him Porphyry. The longer form calls him a true foster-son of Pamphilus, not quite eighteen, skilled in fine writing (Martyrs of Palestine, longer form, cic/texts/eusebius_werke-bd2-2-historia-ecclesiastica-vi-x-rufinus-x-xi-grc-lat_schwartz-mommsen1908.txt lines 25247-25248).

lines.text: Seleucus, a confessor from the army, brings Pamphilus news of the young man's death and is put to death at once.
Twelve die in all, and Pamphilus is the only presbyter among them. Julian, arriving from abroad, completes the twelve.

lines.text: In his Lives of Illustrious Men, Jerome lists a Defense of Origen under Pamphilus's name, and writes of the twenty-five volumes in Pamphilus's hand that he guards with joy.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 75, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40962-40969

lines.text: Jerome writes that the Hebrew Gospel of Matthew is still kept in the library Pamphilus gathered at Caesarea.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 3, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 39359-39361

lines.text: Rufinus of Aquileia puts the first book of the Defense into Latin, calling it the book Pamphilus is said to have written in Greek.
lines.reference: Rufinus, preface to his Latin of the Defense, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 45144-45147

lines.text: In his Letter 84, Jerome asks how he can know the book is Pamphilus's, and suggests it belongs to Didymus or someone else.
Rufinus answers that Jerome no longer spares even the martyrs.

lines.when: About ten years after his catalog
lines.text: Jerome says the Defense is the first of Eusebius's six books, that he found the six volumes in the library at Caesarea, and that Rufinus changed a few statements about the Son of God and the Holy Spirit.
lines.reference: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 51376-51388 and 54976-54980

lines.when: About ten years after his catalog
lines.text: Jerome complains that readers give no heed to the bishops who condemn Origen, since they think a martyr has praised him.
lines.reference: Jerome, Apology against Rufinus I.10, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 51453-51456
lines.note: Jerome dates his catalog about ten years before (Apology against Rufinus, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 53975-53981).

timeline.when: The fifth to the ninth century
timeline.headline: Remembered as martyr, teacher and founder of a library

lines.text: Socrates of Constantinople calls Pamphilus and Eusebius trustworthy witnesses for Origen, in their joint life and defense of him.
Gennadius lists among Rufinus's Latin translations a work of Pamphilus the Martyr Against the mathematicians.
lines.reference: Gennadius, Lives of Illustrious Men 17, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 42472-42476

lines.text: Isidore of Seville says Pamphilus was the first among Christians to try to equal Pisistratus in zeal for a sacred library, and that he had nearly thirty thousand volumes.
lines.note: The thirty thousand is Isidore's alone.

lines.text: A Syriac chronicle says Pamphilus taught Eusebius, who was surnamed Pamphilus after him, and that he suffered martyrdom in this time.
Theophanes lists Pamphilus, presbyter of Caesarea, among the martyrs of the persecution.
lines.note: Held in a damaged Latin print.

lines.text: Photius reads the six books of the Defense, and says five were written by Pamphilus in prison and the sixth by Eusebius alone after Pamphilus's death.
